idiom_name: one stage class per step + rvalue-qualified [[nodiscard]] setters returning the next stage
implementation_notes: Each step is a small class holding the partially built state; its transition is rvalue-qualified (&&) so the intermediate builder cannot be reused after the step, and it returns the next stage type, so build() exists only on the final stage. This is the direct C++ transcription of the Java interface chain and works on any C++11 toolchain ([[nodiscard]] needs C++17 and is simply omitted before that). Prefer it when portability matters and the number of steps is small; C++20 designated initializers are not a substitute, because they fix declaration order but still allow fields to be omitted.
pitfalls: C++ values are copyable: the &&-qualified setter only *conventionally* consumes the intermediate builder, so bind it to a variable and the stale stage can still be advanced - delete the copy/move operations of intermediate stages to make the transition real.
Forgetting [[nodiscard]] (or being on C++11/14) lets `builder.host("x");` silently drop the transition, leaving an unmodified builder and no diagnostic.

Stage classes must carry the accumulated state, so passing them by value copies it at every step; for large payloads move the state into the next stage explicitly instead of relying on implicit copies.

variants.name: Template type-state with a tag pack (C++20)
variants.idiom_name: Builder<Tags...> with a requires-clause on build()
variants.implementation_notes: One class template parameterized by the tags of the steps already applied: every setter returns Builder<Tag<step>, Tags...> and build() is constrained with a requires-clause over the pack, so a missing step is a named unsatisfied-constraint diagnostic instead of a missing member. Unlike the staged form this allows a free step order and can also forbid double application (a tag already present in the pack fails a static_assert); the trade-off is template machinery and less readable signatures. Pre-C++20 toolchains must fall back to the staged-types variant or to static_assert/SFINAE.
pitfalls: The constraint is only as good as its tag list: forgetting to add a new tag to the requires-clause leaves build() callable without the step.
Error messages name the unsatisfied constraint rather than the workflow step; give each stage a named concept or tag type with a readable name so the diagnostic is actionable.
Tag types must be non-public (or at least not nameable by callers): a caller that can spell Builder<HostTag, PortTag> can construct a value that skipped both steps.
